Log rotation on Linux

logrotate runs from a timer, not from the logging daemon, which is why a service that keeps its file descriptor open needs either copytruncate or a signal to reopen. Getting that wrong produces a file that grows forever while df reports the space as used and ls reports it as gone.

journald sidesteps the whole problem by owning storage itself, with size limits per journal and automatic vacuuming. The tradeoff is a binary format and a query tool you have to learn.

Whichever you use, alert on free space rather than on rotation success. Rotation quietly failing is the normal failure mode, and the disk filling is what actually pages someone.
